said: But what is most important is that you have to dig deep down, dig deep down and ask yourselves, who do you want to be? Not what, but who.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
do: Write one sentence today that names who you are training to become, not the job title you are chasing.

said: I say break the rules. Not the law, but break the rules.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
takeaway: Break the rule that's in your way
do: Drop one unnecessary rule in how you train or work today and do the session the way the goal actually requires.

said: You can't be paralyzed by fear of failure or you will never push yourself.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
takeaway: Make the call you've been dodging
do: Make one decision you have been freezing on and take the first irreversible step before noon.

said: You never want to fail because you didn't work hard enough.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
do: Finish today's main session of work or training so thoroughly that a loss could not be blamed on skipping the hard part.

said: I always believed leaving no stone unturned.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
do: Before you call today's task done, check the one corner you usually skip and do that part too.

said: But when you're out there partying, horsing around, someone out there at the same time is working hard. Someone is getting smarter and someone is winning.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
do: Use one hour tonight that you would have spent drifting, and put it into the craft you say you want.

said: You can't climb the ladder of success with your hands in your pockets.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
takeaway: Put your hands on the work
do: Do one hour of hands-on practice in your craft today, not an hour of watching other people do it.

said: Whatever path that you take in your lives, you must always find time to give something back, something back to your community, give something back to your state or to your country.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
do: Give one hour today to a person or a local place that does not pay you, and leave it better than you found it.

said: He told graduates that the things agents called defects, his body and his accent, became assets only after he trained them on purpose.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
do: Take the trait you have been hiding and spend thirty minutes practicing it in public, a voice, a lift, or a skill.

said: He said he took acting, English, speech, and dialogue classes, and ran lines until the sounds that had blocked him started to work.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
do: Practice one precise line of your craft out loud for twenty minutes until the sound is clean.

said: He said he paid no attention to people who told him a thing had never been done, because doing it would mean he was first.
source_title: University of Southern California commencement address, 2009
takeaway: Do what they said can't be done
do: Write down the one sentence someone used to tell you this cannot be done, then do today's rep of it anyway.

said: My goal for this email is simple: more transparency and less BS.
source_title: Collector's item: the first-ever Pump Daily
do: Tell one person the plain status of a promise you made, with no spin, and name the next action.

said: We send a message to our brain that "I am doing this, whether you like it or not," and it lets us break through the inertia that wants to hold us in our status quo.
source_title: Collector's item: the first-ever Pump Daily
takeaway: Do it, like it or not
do: Do the workout or the page you do not feel like doing, for the time you set, and do not renegotiate it midstream.

said: Negativity freezes you; it makes you depressed about where you are instead of excited about where you can go. Lose the negativity.
source_title: Collector's item: the first-ever Pump Daily
do: Write where you are and where you want to be in honest lines, with no insult aimed at yourself, then stop.

said: Write down the ACTION that moves you toward your VISION. Don't bite off more than you can chew.
source_title: Collector's item: the first-ever Pump Daily
takeaway: Pick one action and finish it
do: Under one vision, write one action small enough to finish today, and do that action.

said: The new you stopped wishing and just started.
source_title: Collector's item: the first-ever Pump Daily
do: Start the thing you have only been wishing for, for five real minutes, before you do anything else optional.

said: He told readers to put three aims where they will see them every day, and to make at least one of them about the body.
source_title: Collector's item: the first-ever Pump Daily
takeaway: Keep your aims where you see them
do: Write three aims on a card, one of them physical, and tape it where you will see it at breakfast.

said: He said to mark the small daily tasks done and to congratulate yourself at the end of the day, because the checked box is the reward that keeps the next day alive.
source_title: Collector's item: the first-ever Pump Daily
takeaway: Check the box and own it
do: Track the three actions you named, check them off tonight, and take one minute to credit the ones you finished.

said: He offered a daily hour with no machine as the concrete action for being present, so that whoever you are with gets all of the attention.
source_title: Collector's item: the first-ever Pump Daily
do: Keep one hour today with the phone out of reach while you are with your family or a friend.

said: You're someone who trains and keeps a promise to yourself.
source_title: The 20-Minute Insurance Policy
takeaway: Keep the promise you made yourself
do: Keep the training promise you made this morning, even if the session is short and ugly.

said: One bad day happens to everybody. But the next day, you get your 20 minutes no matter what.
source_title: The 20-Minute Insurance Policy
do: If you missed yesterday, do twenty minutes of movement today before you negotiate anything else.

said: He said that on filming days he could not always find the perfect gym, so he ran the hotel stairs, and that those minutes were the part of the day he still controlled.
source_title: The 20-Minute Insurance Policy
takeaway: Move hard with what time you have
do: When the schedule is not yours, take the stairwell or the block outside and move hard for the minutes you still own.

said: Stop chasing the ceiling. Start raising the floor.
source_title: Stop Chasing Personal Records: Why Your Minimum Standards Matter More
do: Write the minimum you will not go under today for body, food, and mind, and hit all three.

said: Your floor should feel almost embarrassingly easy. That's why you'll do it.
source_title: Stop Chasing Personal Records: Why Your Minimum Standards Matter More
takeaway: Make your standard easy to hit
do: Lower one daily standard until it is small enough that you will still do it on a bad day, then do it.

said: If you don't do the hard reps, the boring reps, the so-so reps, you don't ever get the chance to do your best reps.
source_title: Stop Chasing Personal Records: Why Your Minimum Standards Matter More
do: Finish the set that feels merely average, because that is the set that keeps the best ones possible.

said: He said discipline is the comeback, not the punishment, and that after a slip you return to the floor as fast as you can.
source_title: Stop Chasing Personal Records: Why Your Minimum Standards Matter More
takeaway: Come back fast after a slip
do: If you already slipped today, do the minimum once more before bed and call the slip closed.

said: I've talked a lot of times about how if motivation is what you seek, you will fall short. Momentum is what you need.
source_title: Arnold's 4 Principles of Unbreakable Routines
do: Start the next small rep while you still have a little momentum, and do not wait to feel motivated.

said: If you don't learn to celebrate every single day, when that motivation runs out, you won't have the internal motivation to keep going.
source_title: Arnold's 4 Principles of Unbreakable Routines
do: Mark today's small win where you can see the tally, and name it a win out loud.

said: You had a stressful day and ate too much? That is today's screwup.
source_title: Arnold's 4 Principles of Unbreakable Routines
do: Write today's miss in one honest line, forgive it, and set tomorrow's first meal or first session before you sleep.

said: Why would I ever stop something that makes my life better?
source_title: Arnold's 4 Principles of Unbreakable Routines
takeaway: Keep doing what makes you better
do: Do the training that makes your life better today, even a short session, instead of deciding you are finished with it.

said: Just use these principles and do something now.
source_title: Arnold's 4 Principles of Unbreakable Routines
do: Do not postpone the restart until a later month: do one rep of the habit in the next hour.

said: My vision right now is to become someone who moves every hour, even if it is just a walk around my yard with the animals.
source_title: Arnold's Step Challenge
do: Stand up once each hour you are awake today and walk, even if it is only around the house.

said: A lifetime in the gym has taught me that small progressions are the key to sustainable success.
source_title: Arnold's Step Challenge
takeaway: Add a little more than yesterday
do: Add about a thousand steps to whatever you already walk today, and do not jump to a number you will abandon.

said: No matter how successful we are, there is something we can all do better. That isn't a failure; it's an opportunity.
source_title: Arnold's Step Challenge
do: Name one ordinary thing you are still bad at and do one small rep of it before tonight.

said: He and his assistant sent each other a photo of their step counts every night so the promise had a witness.
source_title: Arnold's Step Challenge
takeaway: Let someone watch you keep it
do: Send one person your finished count tonight, steps or reps, and ask them to send theirs.

said: Reps are the ONLY antidote to being bad at something.
source_title: The 1-Degree Difference
do: Do the lift or the skill you have been training around, for one honest session, starting light.

said: I cut the legs off of all of my sweatpants so I had to see my calves all day long.
source_title: The 1-Degree Difference
do: Put the weakness you are training where you will see it all day, a note on the mirror or the bar you cannot walk past.

said: Are you afraid to talk to people? Talk more.
source_title: The 1-Degree Difference
do: Have one real conversation you have been avoiding, and stay in it until it is finished.

said: Do you struggle with eating well? Eat more vegetables.
source_title: The 1-Degree Difference
do: Put vegetables on the plate at the next meal before you put anything else there.

said: He said he trained the calves everyone called a weakness every day, and that a year of those reps is what turned them into a strength.
source_title: The 1-Degree Difference
do: Train the body part or skill you are embarrassed by for one hard session today, and log the reps.

said: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.
source_title: Meditations, Book II, translated by George Long
do: Before you leave home, write the three people most likely to irritate you today and the one calm sentence you will use if each of them shows up.

said: Remember how long thou hast been putting off these things, and how often thou hast received an opportunity from the gods, and yet dost not use it.
source_title: Meditations, Book II, translated by George Long
do: Finish today the one task you have postponed longest that can actually be done before night, and do not open a second project after it.

said: Every moment think steadily as a Roman and a man to do what thou hast in hand with perfect and simple dignity, and feeling of affection, and freedom, and justice; and to give thyself relief from all other thoughts.
source_title: Meditations, Book II, translated by George Long
takeaway: Do the job in front of you
do: Give the one job in front of you a single uninterrupted hour, and leave every other thought outside that hour.

said: Remember that all is opinion.
source_title: Meditations, Book II, translated by George Long
takeaway: Separate the fact from your story
do: When one remark stings today, write the plain fact on one line and your added opinion on the next, then act only from the fact.

said: Do not waste the remainder of thy life in thoughts about others, when thou dost not refer thy thoughts to some object of common utility.
source_title: Meditations, Book III, translated by George Long
do: Each time you start rehearsing what someone else thinks of you, write it down once and replace it with one useful task you finish before evening.

said: If thou workest at that which is before thee, following right reason seriously, vigorously, calmly, without allowing anything else to distract thee, but keeping thy divine part pure, as if thou shouldst be bound to give it back immediately; if thou holdest to this, expecting nothing, fearing nothing, but satisfied with thy present activity according to nature, and with heroic truth in every word and sound which thou utterest, thou wilt live happy.
source_title: Meditations, Book III, translated by George Long
takeaway: Work one task until it's done
do: Clear the table to one task, work it until it is finished or the hour is up, and do not check whether anyone noticed.

said: Let no act be done without a purpose, nor otherwise than according to the perfect principles of art.
source_title: Meditations, Book IV, translated by George Long
do: Write the purpose of today's main job in one line before you start, and stop when that purpose is met.

said: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself.
source_title: Meditations, Book IV, translated by George Long
do: Take ten minutes in a shut room with no screen and write the trouble you were about to leave the house to escape.

said: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee.
source_title: Meditations, Book IV, translated by George Long
takeaway: Do the good you've been saving
do: Do one concrete good for another person today that you have been saving for a later, easier week.

said: Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.
source_title: Meditations, Book IV, translated by George Long
do: When the next annoyance hits, wait ten minutes before you answer, write what the wave actually was, then return to the work.

said: Occupy thyself with few things, says the philosopher, if thou wouldst be tranquil.
source_title: Meditations, Book IV, translated by George Long
do: Cross three items off today's list and finish only the one that is actually necessary.

said: Love the art, poor as it may be, which thou hast learned, and be content with it; and pass through the rest of life like one who has intrusted to the gods with his whole soul all that he has, making thyself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any man.
source_title: Meditations, Book IV, translated by George Long
do: Spend one hour on the craft you already know, however plain it is, and do not shop for a new one today.

said: In he morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present- I am rising to the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world?
source_title: Meditations, Book V, translated by George Long
takeaway: Get up and do the work
do: Get up and do the first piece of your real work before you bargain with yourself about whether you feel like it.

said: About what am I now employing my own soul? On every occasion I must ask myself this question, and inquire, what have I now in this part of me which they call the ruling principle?
source_title: Meditations, Book V, translated by George Long
takeaway: Check what your mind is doing
do: Set three alarms today and, at each one, write a single line on what your mind is actually doing.

said: Things themselves touch not the soul, not in the least degree; nor have they admission to the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul: but the soul turns and moves itself alone, and whatever judgements it may think proper to make, such it makes for itself the things which present themselves to it.
source_title: Meditations, Book V, translated by George Long
takeaway: Change your judgment, not the world
do: When something hits you today, write the event and your judgment on two separate lines, and change only the judgment before you reply.

said: Art thou angry with him whose armpits stink? Art thou angry with him whose mouth smells foul?
source_title: Meditations, Book V, translated by George Long
takeaway: Don't judge, just finish the errand
do: The next time someone's manner disgusts you, finish the errand you came for and leave without a comment about him.

said: Let it make no difference to thee whether thou art cold or warm, if thou art doing thy duty; and whether thou art drowsy or satisfied with sleep; and whether ill-spoken of or praised; and whether dying or doing something else.
source_title: Meditations, Book VI, translated by George Long
do: Do today's duty once under the excuse you usually honor, whether you are tired or unpraised, and stop when the duty is done.

said: When thou hast been compelled by circumstances to be disturbed in a manner, quickly return to thyself and do not continue out of tune longer than the compulsion lasts; for thou wilt have more mastery over the harmony by continually recurring to it.
source_title: Meditations, Book VI, translated by George Long
do: After the next upset, give yourself five minutes, then return to the task and do not replay the upset for the rest of the hour.

said: When we have meat before us and such eatables we receive the impression, that this is the dead body of a fish, and this is the dead body of a bird or of a pig; and again, that this Falernian is only a little grape juice, and this purple robe some sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shell-fish: such then are these impressions, and they reach the things themselves and penetrate them, and so we see what kind of things they are.
source_title: Meditations, Book VI, translated by George Long
takeaway: See things for what they are
do: At one meal today, name the food and the clothes as what they are before you use them, and stop when you are fed rather than when you are entertained.

said: If a thing is difficult to be accomplished by thyself, do not think that it is impossible for man: but if anything is possible for man and conformable to his nature, think that this can be attained by thyself too.
source_title: Meditations, Book VI, translated by George Long
do: Pick one hard thing you called impossible, confirm a man has done it, and do the first hour of that same work today.

said: In the gymnastic exercises suppose that a man has torn thee with his nails, and by dashing against thy head has inflicted a wound.
source_title: Meditations, Book VI, translated by George Long
takeaway: Step aside, don't hold a grudge
do: If someone clips you today in work or in play, step out of the way without a speech and do not retell it later as if he were an enemy.

said: Adapt thyself to the things with which thy lot has been cast: and the men among whom thou hast received thy portion, love them, but do it truly, sincerely.
source_title: Meditations, Book VI, translated by George Long
do: Do one unsentimental service today for a person you actually live or work with, and do not announce it.

said: When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee; for instance, the activity of one, and the modesty of another, and the liberality of a third, and some other good quality of a fourth.
source_title: Meditations, Book VI, translated by George Long
takeaway: Tell him what's good in him
do: Write one real virtue of four people around you, and tell one of them that virtue to his or her face today.

said: Accustom thyself to attend carefully to what is said by another, and as much as it is possible, be in the speaker's mind.
source_title: Meditations, Book VI, translated by George Long
do: In one conversation today, repeat the other person's point in a single sentence before you add your own.

said: Is my understanding sufficient for this or not? If it is sufficient, I use it for the work as an instrument given by the universal nature.
source_title: Meditations, Book VII, translated by George Long
takeaway: Do it or hand it off
do: If you can do the job in front of you, do it today; if you cannot, hand it to someone who can before noon and say so plainly.

said: Be not ashamed to be helped; for it is thy business to do thy duty like a soldier in the assault on a town.
source_title: Meditations, Book VII, translated by George Long
do: Ask one person today for a specific help you have been too proud to request, and let him do his part.

said: It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong.
source_title: Meditations, Book VII, translated by George Long
takeaway: Be decent to who wronged you
do: For one person who wronged you, write that he acted in ignorance, then either correct him once kindly or do him one small good and stop.

said: Think not so much of what thou hast not as of what thou hast: but of the things which thou hast select the best, and then reflect how eagerly they would have been sought, if thou hadst them not.
source_title: Meditations, Book VII, translated by George Long
do: List five things you already have that you would scramble to recover, and use one of them on purpose today.

said: Look round at the courses of the stars, as if thou wert going along with them; and constantly consider the changes of the elements into one another; for such thoughts purge away the filth of the terrene life.
source_title: Meditations, Book VII, translated by George Long
takeaway: Look up, then get back to work
do: Step outside once tonight, look up for five minutes with no phone, and come back only to the one task that still matters at that scale.

said: When thou hast done a good act and another has received it, why dost thou look for a third thing besides these, as fools do, either to have the reputation of having done a good act or to obtain a return?
source_title: Meditations, Book VII, translated by George Long
takeaway: Do the favor and keep quiet
do: Do one good turn today and do not mention it or wait around for thanks.

said: Attend to the matter which is before thee, whether it is an opinion or an act or a word.
source_title: Meditations, Book VIII, translated by George Long
do: Finish the one matter already open, whether a decision, a task, or a sentence you owe, and do not start another after it.

said: Thou sufferest this justly: for thou choosest rather to become good to-morrow than to be good to-day.
source_title: Meditations, Book VIII, translated by George Long
do: Do today, in a form that fits before sunset, the good act you had scheduled for a better mood.

said: Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life.
source_title: Meditations, Book VIII, translated by George Long
do: Write only what today requires, ignore the life plan for the rest of the day, and finish that one requirement.

said: A cucumber is bitter.- Throw it away.
source_title: Meditations, Book VIII, translated by George Long
do: Throw out or walk around one irritation today without adding a speech about why the world contains it.

said: Enter into every man's ruling faculty; and also let every other man enter into thine.
source_title: Meditations, Book VIII, translated by George Long
takeaway: Let someone see what you're after
do: Ask one person what he thinks you are optimizing for, write his answer down, and tell him one aim you see in him.

said: To-day I have got out of all trouble, or rather I have cast out all trouble, for it was not outside, but within and in my opinions.
source_title: Meditations, Book IX, translated by George Long
do: Write the trouble you are carrying and the opinion that makes it trouble, then close the page and leave the opinion there.

said: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
source_title: Meditations, Book X, translated by George Long
takeaway: Be the man, skip the speech
do: Cancel one speech about the man you mean to become, and do one unnoticed act that man would do today.

said: For whatever this may be, it is in thy power to do it or to say it, and do not make excuses that thou art hindered.
source_title: Meditations, Book X, translated by George Long
do: Say or do the reasonable next thing on the task in front of you, and do not write an excuse for why today was the wrong day.

said: What is thy art? To be good.
source_title: Meditations, Book XI, translated by George Long
takeaway: Do the work, not the tools
do: Name the one piece of good work your actual trade requires today, and do that piece before you improve your tools.

said: Neither in writing nor in reading wilt thou be able to lay down rules for others before thou shalt have first learned to obey rules thyself.
source_title: Meditations, Book XI, translated by George Long
do: Keep, for this one day, a rule you would give someone else, and give no advice until you have kept it.

said: When a man kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should whisper to himself, "To-morrow perchance thou wilt die."
source_title: Meditations, Book XI, translated by George Long
takeaway: Hold your kid like it's the last
do: Spend one unrushed sitting with your child, or with the person who would miss you, and leave the phone in another room.

said: All those things at which thou wishest to arrive by a circuitous road, thou canst have now, if thou dost not refuse them to thyself.
source_title: Meditations, Book XII, translated by George Long
takeaway: Take the shortcut you've been refusing
do: Do today, in a small finished form, the thing you have been approaching by a long route.

said: If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it.
source_title: Meditations, Book XII, translated by George Long
takeaway: Don't do or say the crooked thing
do: Strike one act and one sentence from today that you already know are crooked, and do not replace them with softer versions.

said: First, do nothing inconsiderately, nor without a purpose. Second, make thy acts refer to nothing else than to a social end.
source_title: Meditations, Book XII, translated by George Long
do: Before the three main acts you take today, write each purpose in a line, and drop any act that serves only against someone else.

said: There are two ways of making a good living. One is the result of hard working, and the other, the result of the imagination (requires work, too of course).
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
takeaway: Work hard, then dream up more
do: Spend one hour doing the plain work of your craft, then spend twenty minutes writing the idea that work is for.

said: In every industry, in every profession, ideas are what America is looking for.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: Write one idea you have not heard anyone else say, in a few clear lines, and put it where you will act on it.

said: There are yet long years ahead of me to polish my techniques and character.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: Polish one technique for thirty focused minutes today, and do not add a new one.

said: I don't really worry about the reward, but to set in motion the machinery to achieve it.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
takeaway: Build the machine, ignore the prize
do: Ignore the prize for one day and set up the next concrete step that makes the result possible, then do that step.

said: My contribution will be the measure of my reward and success.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
takeaway: Measure yourself by what you give
do: Measure today by one contribution you finished, not by what you hope to be paid for it.

said: I am not easily discouraged, readily visualize myself as overcoming obstacles, winning out over setbacks, achieving "impossible" objectives.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: Name one obstacle in today's work and picture the next move past it, then make that move.

said: All in all, the goal of my planning and doing is to find the true meaning in life—peace of mind.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: When the day's work is done, sit for ten quiet minutes and do not fill them with a screen.

said: He wrote Pearl that possessions do not add up to peace of mind unless the energy goes into real accomplishment of the self rather than into neurotic combat.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: Drop one argument you are having only to win, and put that hour into a piece of real work.

said: You see, my will to do springs from the knowledge that I CAN DO.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: Do one thing today you already know you can do, at full effort, so the will has evidence.

said: If you don't aim at an object, how the heck on earth do you think you can get it?
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: Write the object of today's session in one line before you start, and stop when that object is met.

said: Pearl, success comes to those who become success-conscious.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: Read your aim once this morning and once before the work, and do not let the day start without it.

said: He told Pearl he could already see a school of his own, and that practical dreamers do not quit when they still own almost nothing.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: Write the picture of the place or the skill you are building, then do one hour of the unglamorous work that picture requires.

said: He wrote that he practiced gung fu as physical culture, mental training, self-defense, and a way of life, not as a single trick.
source_title: Letter to Pearl, September 1962
do: Train once today so that the body, the attention, and the conduct all get a rep, not only the muscles.

said: I Bruce lee, will be the first highest paid Oriental super star in the United States. In return I will give the most exciting performance and render the best of quality in the capacity of an actor.
source_title: My Definite Chief Aim, January 1969
do: Do today's work at the quality you would be willing to sign your name to, and stop before you add filler.

said: I will live the way I please and achieve inner harmony and happiness.
source_title: My Definite Chief Aim, January 1969
do: Make one choice today that matches the life you wrote down, and decline one that only matches the crowd.

said: He wrote a dated aim with a sum and a year on it, and he signed it, so the wish had a form he could not pretend he had not made.
source_title: My Definite Chief Aim, January 1969
do: Write one aim with a date and a number, sign it, and do one hour of the work that number stands for.

said: Now if you are secure within yourself you treat it very, very, very lightly, because you ask yourself, am I really afraid of that man?
source_title: The Last Interview, Ted Thomas, Hong Kong, 9 December 1971
do: When a challenge or an insult shows up today, ask whether you are actually afraid, and do not perform a fight you do not need.

said: I personally believe that all type of knowledge, I don't care what it is, ultimately means self-knowledge.
source_title: The Last Interview, Ted Thomas, Hong Kong, 9 December 1971
takeaway: Learn what the work says about you
do: After you train or study today, write one sentence on what the work showed you about yourself.

said: I do have a bad temper. A violent temper in fact.
source_title: The Last Interview, Ted Thomas, Hong Kong, 9 December 1971
do: Tell one person you trust the temper or fault you usually hide, in plain words, today.

do: Before a task you usually endure, choose how you will start it and say the choice out loud.

said: That's why making a chore into a choice is so powerful: Because it gives us a chance to assert our control.
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, author of Smarter Faster Better
do: Turn one dreaded chore into a choice by picking the piece you will do first and finishing that piece today.

said: You don't want to be running toward the wrong finish line.
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, Author of Smarter Faster Better
do: Write one sentence on what a productive day means for you this week before you open email.

said: A probabilistic thinker, he says, imagines more than one future for a decision, including a best case and a worst case, and then asks which is more likely.
source_title: A Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist investigated the science of productivity
takeaway: Weigh best case and worst case
do: For one decision due today, write a best case and a worst case and pick the option before you leave your desk.

said: Deterministic thinking would say there's one outcome, probabilistic thinking would say there's multiple outcomes.
source_title: A Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist investigated the science of productivity
takeaway: Plan for more than one outcome
do: List three ways this afternoon could go, mark the most likely, and make one move that improves that future.

said: You can never truly extinguish bad habits. To change a bad pattern, you must insert a new routine into the habit loop.
source_title: A Conversation with Charles Duhigg
takeaway: Swap the routine, keep the reward
do: When the old cue shows up today, keep the reward and run a different routine once, all the way through.

said: If you use the same cue, and provide the same reward, you can shift the routine.
source_title: A Conversation with Charles Duhigg
takeaway: Replace the cookie with a conversation
do: Keep the afternoon cue and the social payoff, and swap the cookie or the phone for a five-minute conversation.

said: Really productive people say, "This is hard, and that's okay."
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, Author of Smarter Faster Better
takeaway: Say it's hard and keep going
do: Stay with one difficult block for the full time you set, and write down that the difficulty is the work, not a reason to quit.

said: What psychological safety does not mean is that everyone feels really copacetic and safe.
source_title: A Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist investigated the science of productivity
do: In one meeting, say the disagreement plainly and stay in the room until the point is heard.

said: He argues that skilled communicators recognize which of three conversations is happening, practical, emotional, or social, and then match it.
source_title: Supercommunicators
takeaway: Know what kind of talk it is
do: Before you answer someone today, name whether they want a decision, a feeling acknowledged, or a question of who they are, and match that.

said: A habit is a behavior that starts as a choice, and then become a nearly unconscious pattern.
source_title: A Conversation with Charles Duhigg
do: Catch one automatic behavior today at the moment it starts and choose the next action instead of riding it out.

said: What I discovered was that the real reason I went to the cafeteria was because it offered an opportunity to see friends.
source_title: Charles Duhigg 5 Tips for Resolutions
takeaway: Get the reward you really want
do: The next time the urge hits, take the reward you actually want, such as a short visit with someone, and skip the old routine.

said: There are some habits, called keystone habits, that can cause a chain reaction through someone's life or an organization.
source_title: A Conversation with Charles Duhigg
takeaway: Start the habit that moves others
do: Pick one keystone you want, exercise or a planning ritual, and do a single rep of it today.

said: But control, on its own, often isn't enough.
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, author of Smarter Faster Better
takeaway: Connect the dull task to the point
do: Before a dull task, write the larger aim it serves in one line, then start the task.

said: While finishing his first book he realized he had not taken a day off in nine months, after hearing that Atul Gawande was busy because he had concert tickets with his kids.
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, author of Smarter Faster Better
do: Put one thing you actually want, a walk, a meal, or time with someone, on today's calendar and keep it.

said: When people start exercising even once a week, he reports, unrelated patterns often shift with it, from food to patience.
source_title: A Conversation with Charles Duhigg
takeaway: Exercise, and watch the rest follow
do: Do one bout of exercise today and note one other choice it makes easier before the day ends.

said: Part of becoming more productive, he says, is asking what you want out of the day, the week, or your life.
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, Author of Smarter Faster Better
takeaway: Ask what you want from today
do: Write what you want from the rest of this day in one sentence and drop one task that does not serve it.

said: The goal of looping isn't parroting someone's words, but rather distilling another person's thoughts in your own language.
source_title: How to Be a Supercommunicator at Work
takeaway: Say it back in your words
do: In one real conversation, restate what you heard in your own words and ask whether you got it right before you add your view.

said: In other words, if we want someone to hear us, we should first prove we hear them.
source_title: How to Be a Supercommunicator at Work
do: Ask one clarifying question, wait for the answer, and do not offer your point until they say you understood.

said: In his example, a manager hears "I'm getting overwhelmed" and answers with a task breakdown, missing that the person asked to be met emotionally first.
source_title: How to Be a Supercommunicator at Work
takeaway: Meet the feeling before the fix
do: The next time someone sounds overwhelmed, say what you think they feel and ask if that is right before you suggest a fix.

said: He suggests asking what is most important to the other person in the discussion, and sharing your own aim first so they can be direct.
source_title: How to Be a Supercommunicator at Work
takeaway: Say what you want, then ask
do: Open one work conversation by stating the outcome you want and asking what is most important to them.

said: If a coworker is grieving, jumping to your own loss steals the focus; a better move is to ask what the days have been like for them.
source_title: How to Be a Supercommunicator at Work
do: When someone tells you something hard, ask what the day-to-day has been like and do not answer with your own story.

said: Teammates need to speak in roughly equal proportion over time, and to show they are listening, including by closing laptops and building on what was just said.
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, author of Smarter Faster Better
do: In today's meeting, close the laptop while one quieter person speaks and repeat their point before you move on.

said: When someone seems upset or distracted, he says the useful move is to stop and ask what is going on inside their head.
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, author of Smarter Faster Better
takeaway: Ask what's going on in his head
do: If someone in your group looks checked out today, pause and ask them what is going on before you continue.

said: One paper published by a Duke University researcher found that more than 40 percent of our daily actions are habits.
source_title: A Conversation with Charles Duhigg
takeaway: Notice what you do on autopilot
do: For one hour, log what you do without judging it, then circle the actions that ran on autopilot.

said: To find the reward, he tried different payoffs on different days: coffee for a lift, an apple for hunger, a walk, until socialization explained the cafeteria trip.
source_title: Charles Duhigg 5 Tips for Resolutions
do: Run one reward test today: when the urge hits, try a different payoff and write whether the craving actually drops.

said: Cues, he says, can be a time of day, an emotional state, or another trigger, and his cookie urge kept arriving around 3:30.
source_title: Charles Duhigg 5 Tips for Resolutions
do: Note the clock time and your feeling the next time a bad routine starts, and write the cue in one line.

said: If you read something new, he says, put it down and explain it to the person next to you or it stays as information instead of knowledge.
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, author of Smarter Faster Better
do: Explain one idea you are trying to learn, out loud, to another person before the day ends.

said: An innovation broker, in his account, moves an old idea into a new setting rather than waiting for a bolt of originality.
source_title: A Q&A with Charles Duhigg, author of Smarter Faster Better
do: Take one method that already works in another part of your life and apply it once to the problem in front of you today.

said: Psychological safety, as he describes it, is a shared sense that you can take a risk or offer a half-baked idea without unfair punishment.
source_title: A Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist investigated the science of productivity
do: Bring one unfinished idea to a colleague today and ask them to poke a hole in it.

said: Most of the choices we make each day may feel like the products of well-considered decision making, but they're not.
source_title: A Conversation with Charles Duhigg
do: Pick one decision you think you are making freely today and write the cue that usually makes it for you.

said: People who have an internal locus of control believe they have the freedom and the ability to make their own choices and to determine what happens to them.
source_title: A Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist investigated the science of productivity
do: Make one small decision you have been waiting for someone else to make, and tell them you made it.

said: I do an exercise called “fear-setting” at least once a quarter, often once a month. It is the most powerful exercise I do.
source_title: Fear-Setting: The Most Valuable Exercise I Do Every Month
do: Fill one page in three columns for a decision you are avoiding: the worst outcomes, one way to prevent each, and one way to repair it if it happens.

said: On the fear-setting slides from his TED talk, the last page is the cost of inaction, written emotionally, physically, and financially at six months, one year, and three years.
source_title: Fear-setting worksheet from the TED talk
takeaway: Count the cost of doing nothing
do: On one page, write what your days look like in six months, one year, and three years if you leave this decision untouched.

said: The middle page of that same worksheet asks what the benefits might be of an attempt or of a partial success, and he tells people to spend about ten to fifteen minutes there.
source_title: Fear-setting worksheet from the TED talk
takeaway: List what you gain by trying
do: Spend fifteen minutes writing only the benefits of trying, including a partial success, and stop when the timer ends.

said: Do a 2-week test where “no” to ALL cold intros and pitches?
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
takeaway: Say no to every cold pitch
do: For this one day, refuse every cold introduction and unsolicited pitch, and at dusk write whether your anxiety actually dropped.

said: The anxiety is mostly related to email and startups: new pitches, new intros, etc.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Name the one inbox stream that is making you anxious and do not open it until a single end-of-day pass you can finish today.

said: In the same journal page he decided he would not even see new startup or interview email, and that conference calls would be pushed to email or an end-of-day review.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Mute one inbox for the working day and batch whatever is left into one review you complete before you stop.

said: For me, this means at least 3-4 mornings per week where I am in “maker” mode until at least 1pm.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Delete one meeting or coffee from tomorrow morning and do not put anything else in its place.

said: As Brad Feld and many others have observed, great creative work isn’t possible if you’re trying to piece together 30 minutes here and 45 minutes there. Large, uninterrupted block of time — 3-5 hours minimum — create the space needed to find and connect the dots.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
takeaway: Block three hours for real work
do: Block three uninterrupted hours today and spend them on the one piece of work you cannot do in scraps.

said: I miss writing, creating, and working on bigger projects. YES to that means NO to any games of whack-a-mole.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Pick one kind of reactive chore from yesterday and decline or defer every instance of it for the rest of today.

said: Life favors the specific ask and punishes the vague wish.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Replace one vague wish with a specific ask, and send that ask to one person before evening.

said: An investment that produces a massive financial ROI but makes me a complete nervous mess, or causes insomnia and temper tantrums for a long period of time, is NOT a good investment.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
takeaway: Don't trade your sleep for money
do: Name one commitment that pays you and wrecks your sleep or your temper, and write today the boundary or the pause date.

said: In excess, most things take on the characteristics of their opposite.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Name one good thing you now have too much of, and remove one instance of it from today.

said: Dinner with 5 friends fixes it.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Text the friends you would actually want at a table and put one dinner on the calendar today.

said: One blog post fixes it.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Send or publish one short piece of your own work today instead of waiting for someone to introduce you.

said: NONE of my best deals (Shyp, Shopify, Uber, Twitter, Facebook, Evernote, Alibaba, etc.) came from cold intros from acquaintances.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
takeaway: Drop the channel that never pays
do: Write your three best opportunities and who actually brought them, then drop the cold channel that has never paid off.

said: If you find yourself using nebulous terms like “success,” “happiness,” or “investing,” it pays to explicitly define them or stop using them.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
takeaway: Spell out what a good life is
do: Write one sentence that defines a good day in concrete terms, and do the first visible piece of it before noon.

said: He wrote that he would accept a mild, temporary drop in quality of life, scored from morale in his journal, for a likely return, and not a deal that makes him a nervous mess.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Score today's morale from one to ten in your journal and name the one input you will change if a deal you do not want is dragging it down.

said: He says he will compulsively check news and market pages even while knowing it is self-sabotage, and that his stomach cannot take that kind of watching.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Log out of one news or market feed for the day, and when you reach for it write the sentence you were about to chase.

said: Early on he only wanted bets he could use himself, products that scratched a personal itch, rather than anything that merely looked impressive.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
do: Either use one tool you keep recommending on a real task today, or stop telling people you use it.

said: He considered keeping Friday office hours for people already in his world instead of taking an endless run of new calls.
source_title: How to Say No When It Matters Most
takeaway: Keep an hour for your people
do: Name one hour for the people you already owe, tell them that is the slot, and take no new call outside it today.

said: I am a human guinea pig and professional dilettante.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Be Tim Ferriss — Freakonomics (#162)
do: Ask one person who is unusually good at a single skill what he actually does, then run that method once before the day ends.

said: I meditate almost every morning for 20 minutes, roughly.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Be Tim Ferriss — Freakonomics (#162)
do: Sit for twenty minutes this morning with a timer, and do not open a message until it ends.

said: He said he journals with a short five-minute journal to set the day's tone, then Morning Pages, a free-association exercise, to get the monkey mind onto paper.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Be Tim Ferriss — Freakonomics (#162)
takeaway: Write it out of your head
do: Fill one short focus page and three unedited pages of free writing, and leave them in the notebook before you start work.

said: Between the journal and lunch he tries to do the creative work, writing or recording, and he pushes admin and housekeeping to the afternoon.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Be Tim Ferriss — Freakonomics (#162)
do: Do the creative task before lunch and finish the administrative chores in one afternoon block today.

said: He said that every night he takes a very hot soaking bath, with no bubbles and no jets.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Be Tim Ferriss — Freakonomics (#162)
do: Take one hot bath tonight with the phone outside the room, and get out when you are warm.

said: He described the kind of training that helps him as moving his body through space, balance or acrobatics, rather than moving a weight around a stationary body.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Be Tim Ferriss — Freakonomics (#162)
do: Do one training session today in which you move your body through space, and stop when the session is finished.

said: Your default answer to almost everything should be no.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Say No (#282)
do: For the rest of today, answer every new request with a clear no unless it is already your job, and skip the long excuse.

said: He describes a refusal he respects: a blanket no-coffee diet or no-conference-call diet for a month, a quarter, or a year, so the no is a policy and not a personal slight.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Say No (#282)
do: Decline every coffee or quick chat asked of you today by naming a no-meeting stretch, and give that time back to your work.

said: He has used, and received, a no-conference diet: last year was over-calendared, so the things that most excited him had no room.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Say No (#282)
do: Cancel or decline one conference, panel, or standing call, and send a one-line policy instead of a maybe.

said: When he says no, he keeps the reason short: his own list is already spawning more tasks, and the answer is no rather than a promise to revisit it later.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How to Say No (#282)
do: Reply to one outstanding request in two sentences at most, that your list is already growing and the answer is no.

said: In a short episode he says that defining your fears, instead of your goals, is what lets you do anything uncommon, and he calls the practice negative visualization.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Episode 17, The Power of Negative Visualization
do: Before you write a goal today, write the worst case in one paragraph, and only then decide whether the goal is worth a day.

said: He says that in one evening he filled a sheet with three columns: the worst cases, what would make each less likely, and the actions that would get him back to where he was.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Episode 17, The Power of Negative Visualization
do: On one sheet tonight, write those three columns for one move you are considering, and stop when the sheet is full.

said: The second practice he describes is rehearsing the worst case: a stretch of the cheapest food and the roughest clothes, while asking whether this is the condition you feared.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Episode 17, The Power of Negative Visualization
do: Eat the plainest cheap meal you can stand today, wear something you would normally hide for one errand, and write whether this was the condition you feared.

said: He says the looping what-ifs that kept him from a retreat were not actionable, any more than a badly defined goal is actionable.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Episode 17, The Power of Negative Visualization
takeaway: Act on the what-if or drop it
do: Take one what-if you have been looping and either turn it into a single action you finish before bed or cross it off as not yours.

said: He says many fears come from undervaluing what you can get back easily, once you have actually practiced going without it.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Episode 17, The Power of Negative Visualization
do: Go without one comfort you are afraid to lose, from this morning until tonight, and write what you used instead.

said: I recently went four weeks without phone, computer, or calendar, while in Indonesia.
source_title: One Month with No Phone, preface by Tim Ferriss
takeaway: Put the phone in another room
do: Leave the phone in another room for one full morning, do the work it usually interrupts, and write what actually broke.

said: In the TED essay he says that thinking your way around a fear works worse than writing without editing, and that you should aim for volume on the page.
source_title: How to push past your biggest anxieties and act
do: Set a ten-minute timer and write every fear about one decision without editing a line, then stop when the timer ends.

said: He says the thing you are putting off is often the phone call or the conversation, and that you should define the worst case, accept it, and do it.
source_title: How to push past your biggest anxieties and act
do: Write the worst realistic outcome of one call you have been avoiding, then place that call today.

said: He repeats a line he says he has heard: a person's success can usually be measured by how many uncomfortable conversations he or she is willing to have.
source_title: How to push past your biggest anxieties and act
do: Have the one uncomfortable conversation you have been dressing up as busyness, and keep it to the sentence you wrote down first.

said: He says that trying to figure fear out alone was a mistake he kept making, and that he got better by asking people who already knew how they handled the downs.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: How the Best Overcome Fear (#291)
do: Ask one person who has already done the hard thing how he handled the fear, and write his answer in your own words before you act.

said: Logotherapy sees the human patient in all his humanness.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Write one sentence today about what the person in front of you needs, not what you need from them.

said: You see, any human being is originally – he may forget it, or repress this – but originally he is a being reaching out for meanings to be fulfilled or persons to be loved.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Write the name of one person you can serve in a practical way today, and do one thing for them.

said: The man on the street, he has always understood what I am saying. He sees that something is missing.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Ask one ordinary person what they are living for this week, and write their answer without improving it.

said: He realizes that he is more than his id, more than his drives.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: When a craving shows up, write the task or the person it is standing in for, and give that an hour instead.

said: I start on the ground that guilt is, a priori, personal guilt.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Write one failure that is actually yours, and do a piece of the repair today.

said: I can be judged guilty only for something I have missed, failed to do.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Name the one omission that is yours today and repair it before night.

said: But in no way can I be regarded as guilty for something an uncle of mine has done, or a grandmother of mine has done.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Set down one blame that belongs to someone else, and write the responsibility that is actually yours.

said: So is it bad to be reconciling?
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Say one reconciling sentence to a person you have been keeping at a distance, and do not add a speech.

said: You are never entitled to place the demand of heroism on any one else, not unless you have been in the same position, facing the same decision, the same way facing death as punishment.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Do the hard thing yourself today instead of telling someone else they should have done it.

said: I do not allow myself to confess personally whether I'm religious or not.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Do today's work in the role you actually hold, and leave the speech about what you believe for another day.

said: He doesn't have opinions; his opinions have him.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Write one opinion that has been using you, and spend an hour on a task instead of repeating it.

said: even a genius cannot completely resist his Zeitgeist, the spirit of his time.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Write one assumption you picked up from the people around you, and test it against one duty you have today.

said: If you call 'religious' a man who believes in what I call a Supermeaning, a meaning so comprehensive that you can no longer grasp it, get hold of it in rational intellectual terminology, then one should feel free to call me religious, really.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
takeaway: Serve something bigger than your mood
do: Write one sentence naming a meaning larger than your mood, and do one act that serves it.

said: And a religious person may identify Supermeaning as something paralleling a Superbeing, and this Superbeing we would call God.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Write the name of what you answer to, and do one act of it before the day ends.

said: Better that they should borrow from logotherapy than use their own nonsense.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Use one true idea you already trust and do the practical thing it implies, instead of hunting a new system.

said: I don't give a damn whether they share my philosophical conviction!
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Help one person with something useful today and skip the argument about whether they agree with you.

said: the person is an individuum: the person is indivisible—it cannot be further subdivided or split, because it is a unity.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Treat the person you will see today as one whole human, and do not reduce them to the role they play for you.

said: As such, the person cannot be completely merged into collective orders—mass, class or race.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
takeaway: Talk to him, not his group
do: Speak to one person today as himself, not as a member of a group you have already judged.

said: Every person is an absolute novum.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
takeaway: Look again at someone you've filed away
do: Look at one person you think you have figured out and write one thing about them you have never noticed.

said: The counter-concept to utility value is dignity; dignity, however, belongs to the person alone and is, by its very nature, independent of all vital and social utility.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
takeaway: Be kind to someone useless to you
do: Do one kindness for someone who cannot be useful to you.

said: Being human is, as I myself repeatedly describe it, in the deepest and ultimate sense being responsible.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Write the responsibility that is yours before noon, and carry out one piece of it.

said: This also means that it is more than merely being free: responsibility includes the what for of human freedom—what the human being is free for, what they decide for or against.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Write what you are free for today, not only what you are free from, and do that thing.

said: Thus, contrary to the psychoanalytic view, the person, as understood by the existential analysis I have attempted to outline, is not drive-determined but meaning-oriented; from the point of view of existential analysis, the person does not strive for pleasure but for value.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Choose the valuable task over the pleasant one for one hour today.

said: Where psychoanalysis sees human existence as governed by a will to pleasure, and Individual Psychology sees it as determined by the "will to power," existential analysis sees it as permeated by a will to meaning.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
takeaway: Work for a meaning you can name
do: Write the meaning you are willing to work for today, in one line, and spend an hour on it.

said: Yet I am not driven to faith in God or to God himself; I must decide for or against him.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Make one conscious decision today about what you will serve, and do the first act of it.

said: To ex-sist is to step out of oneself and face oneself, and the human being does this insofar as, qua spiritual person, it faces itself qua psychophysical organism.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Sit for ten minutes and write one true sentence about the man you were today.

said: An animal is not a person because it cannot rise above itself and face itself.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
takeaway: Cut one thing you did today
do: At the end of the day, write one thing you did and one thing you will not repeat tomorrow.

said: The call of transcendence is heard in conscience.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: When your conscience names one thing, do it before you negotiate with it.

said: Meaning is a wall beyond which we cannot tread further; rather, we must accept it.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
takeaway: Do what's in front of you
do: Stop searching for a total theory of your life tonight and write the demand that is already in front of you.

said: Human existence is always oriented toward meaning, however little knowledge it may have of that meaning.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Do one meaningful act today even though you cannot explain the whole of your life.

said: The building blocks can be passed on—but not the master builder.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
takeaway: Do the part only you can do
do: Do one piece of work today that only you can do, and do not hand it off.

said: Again and again, the "defiant power of the human spirit," as I have called it, must be invoked against the psychophysis, which only appears so powerful.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Do one small act today that your fatigue says you cannot do, and stop when that act is finished.

said: Whether one wants to or not, whether one acknowledges it or not, the human being believes in meaning for as long as it breathes.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Write one reason this ordinary day is worth finishing, and finish one task that matches it.

said: For logotherapy, religion is—and can only be—an object, not a standpoint.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Serve one person today without turning the help into a sermon.

said: In this it agrees with Albert Einstein, for whom to ask the question of the meaning of life is to be religious.
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Write the question your life is asking you today, and answer it with one action rather than a theory.

said: Love is always the relation between an "I" and a "you"; in the psychoanalytic view, all that remains of this relation is the "it"—sexuality—while from the perspective of Individual Psychology, all that remains a ubiquitous sociality—I mean, das Man (one/they).
source_title: Ten Theses about the Person (Salzburg lecture, 1950; English by Franz Vesely and David Nolland, Viktor Frankl Institute)
do: Give one person an hour in which they are not a function, a problem, or an audience.

said: In the interview he keeps returning to a practical turn: stop asking only what you want from life, and ask what this moment is demanding of you.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
takeaway: Ask what today wants from you
do: Write one sentence answering what today is asking of you, and do that thing.

said: He treats happiness as something that shows up after work done for its own sake, not as a target you can chase directly.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
takeaway: Do good and drop the score
do: Do one good thing today with no plan to feel happy about it, and leave the result alone.

said: Faced with a visa and a career abroad, he stayed with the duty he believed he owed his parents.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
do: Give one concrete hour today to a parent or elder instead of to the more flattering opportunity.

said: When he was honored, he pointed back to the people whose risk had made his later work possible, and he thanked them rather than himself.
source_title: Viktor Frankl at Ninety: An Interview (Matthew Scully, First Things, 1 April 1995)
takeaway: Thank the one who carried you
do: Say or send a thank-you today to one person whose effort made your life possible.

said: I'm about action and action means less talking and more doing.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Stop explaining the plan and spend the next hour doing the thing you have been talking about.

said: You have to learn to cap success.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: After today's win, stop the celebration and go do the unglamorous work you have been postponing.

said: He says the knowledge did not come from the applause, so he caps the money and the attention and gets back to the mental lab where nobody is watching.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Turn off social media for the rest of the day and do one hard session alone, with no photo and no post.

said: It's important to stay hungry, but it's important more to stay humble within that hunger.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Do one low-status job today, the cleaning, the setup, or the chore, and do not tell anyone you did it.

said: He points to a Medal of Honor winner who became a janitor and kept picking up the broom, because the second you think you are better than the work, you are lost.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Take the menial task in front of you today and finish it as if the title you want does not exempt you.

said: At the end of the day, I ask myself one question: can I take one more step? And usually the answer is yes.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: When you want to stop the workout or the work today, take one more honest rep before you quit, and only then decide.

said: He says the one-second urge to quit, the cold, the warmth, the wish to go home, is where people lose, and that second can turn into decades of regret.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: The next time you want to quit today, stay in the hard thing for ten more minutes and write where you will be in a year if you walk away.

said: He got off a race when his body was in real trouble, then went back out for the miles that were left because something in him said he was not done, even with no official finish.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Go back today and finish the session you abandoned, even if it no longer counts for anyone but you.

said: You have to learn to perform without motivation.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Train today on the hour you least feel like it, and do not wait for a mood, a playlist, or a reason.

said: He says motivation is only kindling, and you fail when you refuse to study or train on the days the spark is gone.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Do forty-five minutes of the work with no hype and no reward at the end, then stop.

said: That phone is the biggest distraction in the world.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
takeaway: Leave the phone in another room
do: Leave your phone in another room for the next block of work or for the next real conversation.

said: He runs every morning before the world gets in, a minimum of twelve miles right now, because the second he opens the phone the poison starts.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Tomorrow morning, run or train before you touch your phone, and write the distance or time tonight so it is not a negotiation.

said: He says he runs the thing he hates first, then lifts, and he has kept some version of that order for years.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Put the exercise you avoid first on today's list and do it before the one you enjoy.

said: He reorganizes his mind for two hours at night, the way you clear a cluttered garage, so discipline has a shelf when he wakes up.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Tonight, sit for thirty minutes with no input and write down what is cluttering your head, so tomorrow's work has a place to go.

said: He says confidence is the everyday resume of real calluses, the things you know you did, not a speech you give the mirror.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Write five things you have actually finished, not hoped for, and do one more rep today that you can add to that list.

said: Don't make dreams your master.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Turn the dream you keep describing into three tasks, do the first one today, and do not tell anyone the dream.

said: He says talking about the plan and doing the plan spend the same fuel, and the 4 a.m. alarm loses once the story has already paid you.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
takeaway: Do it before you announce it
do: Do not announce today's goal; set the alarm and do the first hour before you mention it to anyone.

said: If you wake up in the morning and you don't want to do something, you don't care enough about yourself.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Do the self-respecting task you have been skipping, the training, the study, or the hard conversation, before noon.

said: He says the only purpose he needs on a day with no race and no school is to get better, and that purpose is him.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Schedule one hour today to get better at your craft with nothing to win, no event, no audience, and no deadline.

said: It's so easy to be great nowadays, my friend, because most people are weak.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Do the extra lonely hour today that the people around you will skip, and do not look for company.

said: I found peace years ago in the battle.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Pick the fight with yourself you have been avoiding, a standard you keep breaking, and keep it for the whole day.

said: He says you have to recall the mind every day, not once a year, because toughness from an old course does not stay unless you requalify it.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Do a short hard thing today that you already know how to do, so the standard gets tested instead of remembered.

said: He looks for the cruel comments on purpose, saves them, and uses them on the days he does not want to work, instead of arguing with the people who wrote them.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Save one criticism that stung, do not reply, and use it as the reason you finish today's hard block.

said: He says most people in a good place try to build you up, and the ones trying to wreck you are usually in a dark place, so he studies them instead of suing or swinging.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Do not answer the person trying to get a rise out of you today; write what their attack is actually about and get back to work.

said: He says he had a blueprint for how not to live by watching his family, and the youngest kid's advantage is sitting back and seeing what not to repeat.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Write one pattern you watched growing up that you refuse to repeat, and break it once in your behavior today.

said: He went back to see his father not for an apology that would excuse him, but to understand the damage and stop passing it on.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Write what you inherited from one hard relationship, what you will not hand to anyone else, and do one thing today that breaks that line.

said: He says owning the embarrassing truth out loud takes the power away from anyone who might use it, the way a rapper burns his own secrets before the battle.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Write the fact about yourself you have been hiding, say it to one safe person today, and stop managing the secret.

said: He says his mother got out on one reason, her kids, and that one thing was enough to build a life on.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Name the one person or duty that is your reason today, and do one concrete thing for them before you chase a second goal.

said: He says he is with the person he is with, and the phone stays off, because being present is the point.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Give someone you love one hour today with the phone silenced in another room, and do not narrate the hour.

said: He says take what he says with a grain of salt and build your own standard, because copying his sentence is not the work.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Write your own non-negotiable for this week in one sentence, and keep it today without borrowing his.

said: He says a cluttered mind is a garage with no place to park discipline, and you cannot stuff a new habit into a head you have not organized.
source_title: David Goggins interview 3 (Joe Rogan)
do: Clear one physical pile and one open loop today, a bill, a message, or a bag, before you add a new habit.

said: He looked in the mirror to face the day he had just lived, not to hunt for a feeling of happiness.
source_title: David Goggins interview 2 (Huberman Lab)
do: Before bed, stand in front of a mirror and say out loud whether you did what you said you would do today.

said: He says the barbaric standard cannot be copied out of a book; it has to be experienced, and even then it is hard to explain without sounding unhinged.
source_title: David Goggins interview 2 (Huberman Lab)
takeaway: Do what no book can teach
do: Do one hard thing today that no book can do for you, a long effort in bad weather or a conversation you dread, and write only what it cost.

said: He says the growth, for him, was in the low-paid, freezing, questioning hours of smoke jumping, not in the speaking fees he turned down.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
takeaway: Work hard where no one's watching
do: Do one hour of useful hard work today that nobody will pay you extra for and nobody will see.

said: He says the first hundred-miler, started with almost no running background, showed him he had been underachieving, and he did not want that pain numbed because it was the proof.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
takeaway: Go past what you're trained for
do: Attempt a workout or work block longer than you think you are trained for, stop if you are actually injured, and write what you learned you can tolerate.
