said: He keeps a rolling account of where he still has to get better, and he deals in the real version of the fear, not a headset pretending to be the ocean.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Write the one real situation you are avoiding, then do a true small version of it today instead of imagining it.

said: He says between the life you are settling for and the greatness you can picture there is a lot of work, and most people stay on the easy side of that gap.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Write the gap between where you are and the standard you claim, and fill one hour of that gap with work today.

said: He says he studies who has good energy and who does not, because he got good at seeing who to trust by watching people instead of hoping.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Spend one conversation today only noticing whether the person builds you up or drains you, and decide if you will see them again this week.

said: He says people who went through training with him still cannot enjoy their lives because of the one moment they quit, and he is what he should have been because he stayed.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Finish the small commitment you are about to abandon today, so you do not spend the evening replaying the quit.

said: He says when you go to war with yourself you find out exactly who you are, and that is the peace, not the couch.
source_title: David Goggins interview 1
do: Choose the uncomfortable standard for the rest of today, the early stop on the scroll, the full workout, or the honest no, and keep it until you sleep.

said: It's important to keep things open ended, so you're constantly discovering.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Spend one hour on the skill you are learning without deciding in advance what the finished piece has to look like.

said: If you go into a book, knowing what it will be, it will die on the vine.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Read for forty minutes in one book you have been avoiding before you write a single sentence about what it is.

said: Writing things out by hand, has a logic to it. It enables me to think more deeply than when I'm sitting there, typing on a computer.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Copy today's working notes by hand for one sitting instead of typing them.

said: I'm not fast, but I'm thorough.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Give one task a full hour and finish it before you open anything else.

said: It's a boring life, but I maintain freshness through the routines.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Repeat yesterday's short stretch and yesterday's hour of practice, and stop when the hour ends.

said: You have to be a bit of a tyrant and know how to say no. It's not easy.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Decline one request today in a single sentence and keep that hour for the work.

said: Your best ideas come to you when you're not thinking about them.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: After the work hour, walk for twenty minutes with the phone in your pocket and write down the one idea that arrives.

said: The greatest power any human can have is the power to ask questions.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Ask one person a question you do not already know the answer to, and write down what they actually say.

said: You can be married to someone for 30-40 years, and you might not even know them.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
takeaway: Learn the person you live with
do: Ask the person closest to you one question about their day that you have never asked, and do not correct them.

said: Empathy is an immense human potential that people rarely tap into.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Write one paragraph tonight describing a hard moment from another person's side, using only what you saw.

said: The worst sin in the world today, is that people feel like they know everything.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Before you give any advice today, write one thing you do not know about the situation.

said: Mistakes and failure are good, if you're able to learn a lesson.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Write one mistake from this week and the single change you will make on the next attempt.

said: We have consciousness, but we're not using it right. We react too much.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: When something irritates you, wait an hour, then write three options and one consequence before you answer.

said: The worst thing you can have in life, is a job you hate, where you have no energy, you're not creative, and you're not thinking of the future. To me, you might as well be dead.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Use one hour nobody else assigns today on the skill you want, even if the rest of the day is spoken for.

said: I can usually tell, almost from reading the back cover or the first five pages, whether a book will have that 'juice'.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Read the first five pages of one book and write yes or no on whether you will finish it.

said: Every time I wrote a chapter in that book, I was reflecting on a situation in my own life.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Write one scene from your own week in plain sentences, with no moral attached.

said: It's delivering the truth as straight as can be, and we don't have enough of that in this culture.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Tell one person one true thing you have been softening, in two sentences, and then stop talking.

said: You want to know as many different people as possible and have broad experiences.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Have one real conversation today with someone whose work is nothing like yours, and write down one thing you noticed.

said: Everything is material.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Write down one ordinary thing you saw or heard today that you could use later.

said: You can't learn quickly unless you're excited about the subject.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Spend one hour on the part of your craft that still makes you lean forward, and stop when the hour ends.

said: In my early 30s, I was writing screenplays for directors and realized that this wasn't where I wanted to be. I was given a chance to write a book and I was so motivated, so hungry, so desperate (that I made it the best book I could write).
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Write the work you already know is not yours, and spend one hour today on the work that is.

said: Make them want to follow you.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Do one visible piece of the shared work yourself today before you ask anyone else to do it.

said: Greene starts the morning with about twenty minutes of basic stretching and a simple sitting practice in which he watches his own thinking.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Sit for ten minutes this morning and write down the thought that keeps returning.

said: He said he exercises every day, swimming or a short yoga routine, even on days he is sick.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Do one physical session today, even a short one, and do not skip it because the day is crowded.

said: He limits the actual writing to about three hours and relies on the limit to stay fresh.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
takeaway: Cap the work at three hours
do: Set a three-hour block for the real work and close it when the block ends.

said: He treats the twenties as an apprenticeship for gathering two or three real skills across different kinds of work.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Practice one concrete skill for one hour today that is not the job you already know how to do.

said: He said the grim jobs, not the glamorous ones, were what taught him patience.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Do the dullest necessary task on your list for forty-five minutes with no soundtrack.

said: He finds the work worth years by noticing where his mind already wants to stay for hours.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Write the subject you would still be reading at midnight, and spend one hour on it.

said: When something in a message provokes him, he waits until the feeling drops before he answers.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Leave the message that irritated you unsent for one hour, then rewrite it in four lines.

said: He judges people by what they do, and by the first instant of the face, more than by the story they tell.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Watch one conversation without performing, and write one thing the person's actions did that their words did not.

said: He treats a moment that breaks someone's usual manner as information, not as a chance to score a point.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Write one sentence about a moment today when someone acted unlike their usual self.

said: He treats social media as a drain on focus and makes time that is deliberately away from it.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Put the phone in another room for one evening and finish one piece of work.

said: He says the feeling of being entitled to a role is the moment the work starts to rot.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Do one unglamorous part of the job yourself today and do not announce that you did it.

said: He thinks people follow the standard you keep, not the speech you give about it.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: Keep one standard you have been preaching, for this whole day, without mentioning it.

said: He holds strong views and still expects a fact to be able to move them.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
takeaway: Name what would change your mind
do: Write your current view of one problem in a sentence, then write the fact that would make you change it.

said: Alive time, in his telling, is the hour no one else is assigning.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Block one hour that nobody else owns and use it only for practice.

said: On a book that has life in it, he reads slowly, marks the margin, and later writes a theme and a note on a card by hand.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Mark one passage worth keeping and tonight write the theme and the point on a card in your own words.

said: He gets people talking about what they want and what they value, and he assumes he does not already know.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
takeaway: Let him talk about his goals
do: Ask one person what they are actually trying to do this year, and do not talk about yourself until they finish.

said: The louder and more certain a voice is, the more he wants a reason before he believes it.
source_title: 52 Lessons from a Conversation with Robert Greene (Steve Glaveski, Future Squared notes, 15 January 2019)
do: When you hear a loud certain claim today, write one question you would need answered before you believe it.

said: He said the culture pushes people to display everything, and that an evening with nothing to perform is part of keeping a self.
source_title: The Knowledge Project: Alive Time vs. Dead Time with Robert Greene (Podcast Notes, 1 July 2018)
do: Spend one evening with people you love and do not perform, post, or explain yourself.

said: You gotta work harder and you gotta work smarter. You got to do both of them.
source_title: Tim Grover - Becoming Limitless
do: Do today's hard session as written, then add one quality rep and cut one junk set before you leave.

said: When I started with him in 2007, my biggest challenge was to get him to stop.
source_title: Tim Grover Q&A: Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and Winning
takeaway: Stop when the plan says stop
do: Stop one workout at the planned dose today instead of adding extra work because you feel behind.

said: I've never had to tell him to show up early, never had to tell him to stay late or tell him to work hard.
source_title: Tim Grover Q&A: Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and Winning
do: Be at the session ten minutes early, finish the standard you wrote down, and log the result.

said: He counted steps and which leg an athlete loaded, then built the next day's session to balance the side they overused.
source_title: The Price Of Winning & Why It's Worth It
do: Count one imbalance in today's training, left versus right or easy versus hard, and write the adjustment for tomorrow.

said: You get people that say you don't have to work harder, you gotta work smarter, and he rejects the trade.
source_title: Tim Grover - Becoming Limitless
takeaway: Add load to what you know
do: Raise the load on one exercise you already know and keep the rest of the session exactly as planned.

said: Showing up is none of the battle.
source_title: Tim Grover Q&A: Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and Winning
takeaway: Do the work after you arrive
do: After you arrive, complete the first hard block before you check your phone.

said: His preparation, Grover says of Jordan, started when he woke up: the meal, the clothes, the car, so the game day was not a pile of small decisions.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Lay out tomorrow's clothes, food, and first task tonight so the morning starts without a decision.

said: Every single one of your plans should be a plan A.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Throw out the backup excuse for today's main task and do that task as the only plan.

said: If I tell myself it's going to be a great day, it puts me in the correct mindset.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Before the first demand of the day, decide the standard for the next two hours and start on it.

said: He says a routine exists so the bombs in your head, tickets, clothes, where to be, do not go off on the day that matters.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Clear three small open loops before the important block so they are not in your head while you work.

said: Pressure is a privilege.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Take the hard conversation or the hard set you have been avoiding and finish it today.

said: Stress is just pressure that you didn't decide to deal with.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Name one pressure you have been calling stress and handle the next concrete step of it before evening.

said: Don't go with anger. Go with controlled rage.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: When you get hot today, wait until you can state the decision in one calm sentence, then act on that sentence only.

said: Don't play with emotions. Play with energy.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Do the work block at a steady pace and do not let a mood change the plan mid-set.

said: Your mind has to be stronger than your feelings.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
takeaway: Make the call you know is right
do: Make the decision you already know is right and send it or do it before you talk yourself out of it.

said: When you get knocked down there, stay down for a little bit.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: After a miss today, sit with what put you there for twenty minutes and write the cause before you start the next attempt.

said: It's not about the glamour. It's not about the glory.
source_title: Tim Grover Q&A: Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and Winning
do: Do the unglamorous piece of the work, the extra set or the dull review, and do not post about it.

said: They're not looking for motivation. They're looking for elevation.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Start the first ten minutes of the hard thing without a pep talk, playlist speech, or waiting to feel ready.

said: It's okay to have fear, but winning doesn't want you to have doubt.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Do the thing you are afraid of once today, and do not add a speech about whether you are the kind of person who can.

said: There is no one thing.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Finish one necessary step on the path you actually want, then write the next step so it is waiting tomorrow.

said: You know how you get closer to balance, you get rid of the unessentials.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Cancel or delete one commitment today that does not move the result you say you want.

said: He treats every decision as having a cost, and says the price of regret can run higher than the price of winning.
source_title: The Man Who Coached Michael Jordan AND Kobe Bryant To WIN! Tim Grover
do: Write what today's goal costs you, time or comfort, and pay that cost once before you renegotiate it.

said: Be with your clients through the good and the bad.
source_title: Tim Grover Q&A: Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and Winning
do: Contact one person you work with who is struggling and ask what they need done, then do one piece of it.

said: The truth should lead to more action and better results.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Tell one person the uncomfortable fact they need, and name the action that follows before the conversation ends.

said: In any relationship, he says, people ask for honesty and then flinch, so he tells them he is there to raise performance, not to judge them.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Ask someone you trust to name one thing you are doing that is hurting the result, and do not argue for ten minutes.

said: He describes telling his daughter, while packing for another trip, that he was leaving to provide and to show what it looks like to keep a commitment.
source_title: The Price Of Winning & Why It's Worth It
do: Tell the person your schedule affects why you are choosing the work today, in plain language, before you leave.

said: Michael would not ask teammates to do what he would not do himself, and sometimes he sent Scottie to deliver the message because his own tone would backfire.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
takeaway: Don't demand what you won't do
do: Do the task you are about to demand of someone else, or ask the person they will actually hear to say it.

said: Winning isn't heartless, but you'll use your heart less.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Make one people decision with the result in mind, tell them directly, and do not soften it into a maybe.

said: Control your thoughts, you control your emotions, you control your actions.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Write the thought, the feeling, and the one action, then do only the action.

said: I want them to only access their dark side as long as they can control their dark side.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
takeaway: Aim the anger at the work
do: Use the anger for one focused block of work, then stop when the block ends instead of letting it run the evening.

said: It's what keeps you going when nothing else will.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: On the hour you want to quit, do the minimum standard you set this morning and then stop.

said: It stopped when I realized I was the monster.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Write the part of you you usually blame on someone else, and choose one behavior today that keeps it useful instead of in charge.

said: You gotta have that resiliency over and over again.
source_title: Tim Grover - Becoming Limitless
takeaway: Get back on the failed drill
do: Come back to the same drill you failed earlier and complete one clean rep before you go home.

said: After a loss, he says, do not pop back up as the same person; stay down long enough to learn why you were there, then stand up different.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Review today's mistake the same day, write one change, and run that change once before you sleep.

said: The minute the win lands, he says the useful question is what is next, not another round of applause.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: When you finish something today, write the next target in one line before you tell anyone.

said: MJ would have been the greatest basketball player with or without me.
source_title: Tim Grover Q&A: Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and Winning
do: Do your part of the work today and do not spend the session explaining why someone else should carry it.

said: A cooler shows up and leaves on the clock, a closer delivers until too many variables hit, and a cleaner still delivers.
source_title: Tim Grover - Becoming Limitless
do: When the plan breaks today, change one variable and finish the outcome instead of stopping at the excuse.

said: Winning wants all of you. There is no balance.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
takeaway: Guard two hours for the win
do: Protect a two-hour block for the one result and decline one pleasant thing that collides with it.

said: I don't have everything I want, but I have more than what I need.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
do: Choose sleep or food you actually need over one optional extra session, and keep that recovery choice.

said: You bring me in to clean things up.
source_title: Tim Grover | The Unforgiving Race to Greatness
takeaway: Strip out what doesn't earn its place
do: Remove one person, tool, or habit from today's plan that you cannot justify, and work without it.

said: If you do not work on an important problem, it's unlikely you'll do important work. It's perfectly obvious.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Work on a problem that matters
do: Write the problem you will touch today and, if you cannot name an attack or a path to something important, switch to one problem that has both.

said: Important here means you have a reasonable attack, not that the prize or the payoff would be enormous if the thing were ever solved.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Drop the problem you can't attack
do: Cross one glamorous problem off today's list because you have no attack, and work an hour on a smaller problem you know how to enter.

said: Great scientists keep something like ten or twenty important problems in mind and drop other work when an attack appears.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Keep a short list of big problems
do: Write ten problems worth your attention and star only those with an opening, then spend one hour on a starred one.

said: People who work with the door shut get today's tasks done and, years later, are often working on a slightly wrong problem.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Open the door for an hour
do: Leave one hour today interruptible, talk to whoever comes by or whom you invite, and write down any clue about what is actually worth doing.

said: Luck favors the prepared mind: the particular thing you hit may be luck, and that you hit something is not.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Spend one hour getting ready for a break you cannot schedule, by learning the piece you would need if it arrived tomorrow.

said: A life of unconnected choices wanders like a random walk, while a vision makes the distance add up instead of cancelling.
source_title: Dr. Hamming's 1990 NPS SGL Lecture
do: Write in one sentence where you want the work to be in a year, and do one step today that walks in that direction rather than a side errand.

said: Short-range forecasts run optimistic because researchers must feel they will finish, and the day itself usually delivers less.
source_title: Dr. Hamming's 1990 NPS SGL Lecture
do: Cut today's plan until it is smaller than your optimism, and finish that shorter list.

said: You have one life, so you should say to yourself that you want to do something significant, even if you do not announce it.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Write the significant thing you want from this life in one private sentence, then spend two hours on a piece of it.

said: What feels like ideal comfort often sterilizes the work, and some of the best physics was done in poor conditions.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Do one important hour today in the conditions you already have, and do not wait for a cleaner room, a better tool, or more time.

said: What looked like a defect, not being given a crowd of programmers, became an asset once the problem was turned around so the machine wrote the programs.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Turn the limit into the method
do: Take one constraint that is blocking you, rewrite it as the method, and use that method on the task today.

said: Drive, applied to the right problem, compounds: a little more thinking, day after day, outproduces equal talent that does less.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Add one extra hour of real thinking today on the problem that matters, and protect it from mail and meetings.

said: Emotional commitment feeds the subconscious, which will work the problem overnight only if nothing else is allowed at the center.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Hand your mind one problem tonight
do: Before sleep, write the one problem in a sentence, refuse every other puzzle for the evening, and look at the page again in the morning.

said: There are people who cause things to happen, people who watch, and people who do not notice, and the first group is a choice.
source_title: Dr. Hamming's 1990 NPS SGL Lecture
do: Cause one concrete result today that would not have happened if you had only watched.

said: What knowledge is worth knowing, given more of it than you can hold, is answered by what you actually study.
source_title: Dr. Hamming's 1990 NPS SGL Lecture
do: Choose one subject to learn for an hour today and explicitly drop one other subject you will not touch.

said: Eating with people outside your own table is how you learn which problems in the next field are actually important.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Talk to someone outside your field
do: Have one meal or long conversation today with someone outside your specialty, and ask what problem in their field is worth an attack.

said: You have to sell the work: clear writing, a formal talk, and the nerve to speak in the middle of a live meeting.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Explain one result today in a page or a five-minute talk that a non-specialist can follow, and send it to one person.

said: Back-room objections that arrive after the decision do not count, so the informal remark in the meeting is part of the job.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: In one meeting today, say the objection when it matters, in a few sentences, instead of saving it for a note afterward.

said: Talk to people who answer back with another idea, and avoid the pleasant listeners who only absorb what you say.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Take one half-formed idea to a person who will argue with you today, and write down the objection you cannot dismiss.

said: You can educate a boss with one visible demonstration more reliably than with a complaint.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Show one decision-maker a finished small result today instead of asking permission for the whole program.

said: Working with the system, rather than fighting it for total control, is what lets the system carry you farther than you can carry yourself.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Use one existing process, colleague, or tool today to move a task, and stop doing that task single-handedly.

said: A small, friendly effort with the people who actually run the place later returns as help you could not have ordered.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Be good to the people behind you
do: Do one concrete kindness today for someone whose work makes yours possible, with no request attached.

said: Friday afternoons were reserved for great thoughts only, about where the field was going, which is a commitment of time to importance.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Block the next unscheduled hour for big questions only, write where your field is going, and do no small tasks in that hour.

said: If you believe the action is in one direction and you spend the week marching in another, change what you do.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Spend your week where you aim
do: Compare today's calendar with the direction you say matters, and move one block onto that direction before noon.

said: About half the time belongs to presentation, because unread work does not enter the cumulative record.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Polish the work to be used
do: Spend as long polishing one result today as you spent producing it, and stop when a stranger could use it.

said: If you read only for other people's solutions you will think their thoughts, so get the problem clear and sit with your own attack first.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Read only enough of one paper or chapter to see the problem, close it, and write your own approach before you look at the answer.

said: Ego assertion, in dress or in a hundred other habits, charges a small steady tax, while the appearance of conforming spends that tax on the work.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Drop one ego habit today that creates friction with the people you need, and spend the recovered attention on the problem.

said: Anger is a poor way to handle the system, and amusement plus cooperation wastes less of the life.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: When you get angry at a process today, write the joke version and the next useful step, and do the step.

said: Great scientists tolerate ambiguity: they believe a theory enough to move and doubt it enough to see the misfit.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Write one flaw in the idea you are using today and keep working without forcing the flaw to vanish before evening.

said: Knowledge and productivity compound, so the person who gets in a little more thinking over years outproduces an equal.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Study the foundation of your craft for one hour today, on purpose, and note one thing you can do afterward that you could not do this morning.

said: Change the question from the isolated job in front of you to the class of jobs, and do this one so the next ones are easier.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Solve today's task in a form you can reuse, and file the method where you will find it next time.

said: It is a poor workman who blames his tools; alter the problem or the viewpoint and get the best answer the tools allow.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Ship one useful result today with the tools already on your desk, and do not spend the day acquiring a new one.

said: Do the work so others can stand on it, because the point of the report is that the next person need not start over.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Rewrite one note or result today so a colleague could continue from the last line without asking you what you meant.

said: Plant small acorns: after early success the failure mode is refusing small problems and waiting for a giant one.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Start one small problem today that could grow, and spend an hour on it even if it will not make your name.

said: Courage in Shannon's style was asking the question that seemed impossible, such as what an average random code would do.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Write the question you have been unwilling to ask on your problem, and spend one hour attacking that question directly.

said: A simulation is not evidence until you can say the calculation is correct and the model matches a real measurement.
source_title: Dr. Hamming's 1990 NPS SGL Lecture
do: Take one model or spreadsheet you trust, check it against one real number today, and write whether it still stands.

said: If you want a no, ask; if you want the thing done, do it and present the accomplished fact.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Finish one small piece of work you have been waiting to get approved, and show the result instead of requesting permission.

said: Very few people can both reform the whole system and do first-class work, so choose which person you are today.
source_title: You and Your Research
takeaway: Pick the work over the fight
do: Drop one fight with the system today and use that hour on the work you say you want to be known for.

said: Do not give yourself the alibi: you can tell it to others if you must, but to yourself say why you were not first and what you will do.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Write the excuse you would offer for a delay, cross it out, and do the delayed action today.

said: He put his pride on a public promise so the ego would force the work, including telling friends the book would be done.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Tell one person a specific result you will hand them today, then do the work that makes the promise true.

said: Every seven years or so, the advice was to shift fields enough to become a beginner again and plant new acorns.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Spend two hours today as a beginner in an adjacent problem, and write what you do not know yet.

said: When the vision is bigger than what you can do alone, management is the tool; when it is not, stay with the work you can do single-handedly and be conscious of the choice.
source_title: You and Your Research
do: Decide in one sentence whether today's goal is a solo work goal or a goal that needs other people, and act only on that side.

said: Bureaucracy can turn a mob into a coordinated effort, and it also answers local crises with petty rules, so ask what should happen, not only what the rules will produce.
source_title: Dr. Hamming's 1990 NPS SGL Lecture
do: Write what your team or household should be doing, then take one permitted step today that moves toward that rather than toward the nearest rule.

said: Prediction fails on the unexpected, so the use of a vision is not to be right about 2020 but to keep your choices from cancelling.
source_title: Dr. Hamming's 1990 NPS SGL Lecture
do: Make one decision today that still helps under two different futures, and write both futures in a line each.

said: Each morning, usually after a long walk on my farm, I go upstairs to my office and pull out three small notebooks.
source_title: This Is The Most Important Thing You Can Do Each Morning
do: After a walk, write one sentence about the day that just passed before you touch a screen.

said: In the second notebook he writes about two pages on yesterday's workout, the work he did, what he is grateful for, what he wants to get better at, and where he is succeeding.
source_title: This Is The Most Important Thing You Can Do Each Morning
do: Fill two pages on yesterday: the workout, the work, one gratitude, and one thing you want to get better at.

said: He finishes with a short prompt, the kind that asks where he is standing in his own way or what smaller step he can take toward a big thing today.
source_title: This Is The Most Important Thing You Can Do Each Morning
do: Answer one hard prompt in writing this morning, such as the smaller step toward a big thing, and do that step today.

said: There’s no right way to do it. Just do it.
source_title: This Is The Most Important Thing You Can Do Each Morning
do: Start in whatever notebook is already in the house, write one page, and do not buy a better system first.

said: I journal each morning as a way of starting the day off fresh—I put my baggage down on the page so that I don’t have to carry it to meetings or to breakfast with my family.
source_title: 10 Ways to Find Stillness in Turbulent Times
takeaway: Put your baggage on the page
do: Before breakfast, write the worry you would otherwise carry into the first conversation, and leave that page at the desk.

said: He says the first thing to filter if you want equanimity is the news, because watching it in real time is not how you stay informed or get anything done.
source_title: 10 Ways to Find Stillness in Turbulent Times
do: Do not open a news site or broadcast today, and put that time into one piece of work you can finish.

said: He says that if you are stressed you should stop and sit down with a book, the kind a writer poured a life into, not the thing trying to pull your attention apart.
source_title: 10 Ways to Find Stillness in Turbulent Times
do: When you are spun up today, read twenty pages of a real book before you go back to a feed.

said: Taking a walk works on a racing or miserable mind just as well as a colicky baby.
source_title: Take A Walk: The Work and Life Benefits of Walking
do: When you are stuck or miserable today, walk until the feeling changes or thirty minutes pass, whichever comes first.

said: He says you do have time to walk: get up earlier, take the phone call outside, do a lap of the lot, or walk instead of calling a car.
source_title: Take A Walk: The Work and Life Benefits of Walking
do: Take the one call you must make while walking outside, and end it when you are back at the door.

said: Where is all this rushing taking you?
source_title: Can You Be Still?
do: Write where today's rushing is actually pointed, and cancel one movement that does not go there.

said: Although I certainly read more on some days than others, I work hard to make sure I read something every day.
source_title: This Is What You Should Read Every Day
do: Read a few pages of a real book today, at a meal or before bed, and mark one line worth keeping.

said: He says each morning you should plan how you mean to act, including the people you will meet and the difficulties, instead of winging it.
source_title: 13 Life-Changing Habits To Try And Do Every Single Day
do: Before you leave, write the people and difficulties you are likely to meet today and the response you will use.

said: He says you must make an hour or more for deep work, and that it starts by closing the browser and getting to it.
source_title: 13 Life-Changing Habits To Try And Do Every Single Day
do: Close the browser and give one hour to the hardest piece of work you have, with the phone in another room.

said: He says to practice one kindness a day, because you will not meet every chance and you should not whip yourself for that.
source_title: 13 Life-Changing Habits To Try And Do Every Single Day
do: Do one deliberate kindness today for someone you did not have to help, and do not post it.

said: He says strenuous exercise needs a number, so that whatever else the day does, you improved a time, a distance, or a weight.
source_title: 13 Life-Changing Habits To Try And Do Every Single Day
takeaway: Put a number on the workout
do: Do one hard workout today with a number on it, a time, a distance, or a weight, and write the number down.

said: I keep a coin in my pocket to remind me of this and touch it at least once a day.
source_title: 13 Life-Changing Habits To Try And Do Every Single Day
do: Carry one small reminder that you will die, touch it once today, and then do the task you have been treating as if you had forever.

said: At night he wants you to go back over what you did and said, hiding nothing, and ask what you will do better tomorrow.
source_title: 13 Life-Changing Habits To Try And Do Every Single Day
do: Tonight, write what you did, what you said, and one thing you will do better tomorrow.

said: He says the other habits collapse if you will not sleep, and that a night's sleep is an obligation rather than a badge of toughness.
source_title: 13 Life-Changing Habits To Try And Do Every Single Day
do: Set a bedtime that gives you a real night, and be in bed then with the phone charging outside the room.

said: One does not need to be an egotistical asshole to be successful.
source_title: Why Ego is The Greatest Opponent to Your Creativity and Success
do: Do today's best work without telling anyone how important it is, and let the work be the only announcement.

said: Confidence is calm, compassionate, curious, careful.
source_title: Why Ego is The Greatest Opponent to Your Creativity and Success
do: In one hard conversation today, slow down, ask one real question, and drop the performance.

said: He says a creative person has to stay humble enough to hear a correction, because ego will not let you see the work or the people it is for.
source_title: Why Ego is The Greatest Opponent to Your Creativity and Success
do: Ask one person to mark a flaw in something you made, write the note down, and change one line before the day ends.

said: Personally, I fiercely protect my mornings—family first, then writing.
source_title: The Secret To Better Habits In 2025
do: Give the first quiet part of the morning to your family and then to the real work, and let calls wait until later.

said: He does not let anything be booked before mid-morning, because an early call spends the energy the essential work needed.
source_title: The Secret To Better Habits In 2025
do: Move any call out of the first half of the morning, and keep that block for the work that actually matters.

said: I don’t have goals. When I write, I don’t focus on finishing books—that would be overwhelming.
source_title: The Secret To Better Habits In 2025
takeaway: Trust the process, not the goal
do: Work the process for two hours, the cards or the next pages, and do not check whether the big project is finished.

said: I don’t keep social media apps on my phone—they’re on my wife’s phone instead.
source_title: The Secret To Better Habits In 2025
do: Remove one social app from your phone today, or put it where you have to ask someone else before you open it.

said: He leaves the journals on the desk so that skipping them means picking them up, and most mornings he writes instead of moving them.
source_title: The Secret To Better Habits In 2025
takeaway: Put the notebook in your way
do: Put the notebook where you cannot sit down without moving it, and write in it before you move it aside.

said: He says you get a double satisfaction from doing less, and he points to people who quit side projects so they could do a few things well.
source_title: The Secret To Better Habits In 2025
do: Resign from one obligation today, in a single sentence, so you can do the remaining work properly.

said: But I do have an expensive habit: anxiety.
source_title: The Secret To Better Habits In 2025
do: Write one hour anxiety has already stolen, and spend that hour today with the person or the work you were too worried to enjoy.

said: He says no is a complete sentence: do not say maybe, do not pile up reasons, and do not push the ask to later.
source_title: The Secret To Better Habits In 2025
do: Say no once today in a complete sentence, with no maybe and no stack of excuses.

said: He says there is no shame in needing help, a comrade or someone who knows more, and that pride should not stop the ask.
source_title: The Secret To Better Habits In 2025
do: Ask one person for a specific help you have been doing badly alone, and let him do that part today.

said: Get in the habit. If you have an idea, put it on a damn card.
source_title: The Notecard System: The Key For Remembering, Organizing And Using Everything You Read
takeaway: Put the idea on a card
do: Write one idea or one quote on a card today, mark a theme in the corner, and put it where you will see it again.

said: He marks pages as he reads, waits a few weeks, and only then copies onto cards the lines that still matter, because the wait is the edit.
source_title: The Notecard System: The Key For Remembering, Organizing And Using Everything You Read
do: If a book has been finished for a couple of weeks, copy one passage that still matters onto a card today and throw out a mark that does not.

said: When he reads he folds the corner of a page that matters and marks the passage, then moves it by hand into the commonplace, because typing is too easy.
source_title: How And Why To Keep A Commonplace Book
takeaway: Mark it and copy it by hand
do: Fold or mark one page that struck you, and copy that passage by hand before you sleep.

said: He says he ruins the ending on purpose, so the reading can be about what the claim means and whether he agrees.
source_title: Read to Lead: How to Digest Books Above Your Level
takeaway: Know the claim, then test it
do: Before you go on with a hard book, read a short account of its claim, then read to decide whether the claim is true.

said: Before he closes a book he rereads what he marked, and he tries to take the next book from that book's bibliography.
source_title: Read to Lead: How to Digest Books Above Your Level
do: Reread the passages you marked in the current book, and write down the one title from its bibliography you will open next.

said: You can’t solve a problem you don’t understand.
source_title: Do You Know How To Do A Deep Dive?
do: Read one serious source on the problem in front of you, not a summary, and write the nub of it in a sentence before you act.

said: He says going deep means swarming the subject, including the people you disagree with and time in the actual place, not stopping at the gist.
source_title: Do You Know How To Do A Deep Dive?
do: Spend two hours today on one subject only, including one source you expect to disagree with, and write what you still do not know.

said: Do one thing in the morning before checking email.
source_title: My Morning Routine
do: Do one real thing, a shower, a run, or a page of writing, before you open email today.

said: The idea is that the phone answers to me rather than the other way around.
source_title: My Morning Routine
takeaway: Make the phone answer to you
do: Turn off alerts that are not a real call, and check the phone on your schedule today rather than when it lights up.

said: For several evenings he and his four-year-old went fishing for a few minutes after dinner, a small repeated thing with someone at home.
source_title: 10 Ways to Find Stillness in Turbulent Times
takeaway: Put the phone down after dinner
do: After dinner, spend a few minutes on one simple thing with someone in your house, and leave the phone behind.

said: Volume negates luck.
source_title: TBPN Live — Alex Hormozi's Playbook for Building Billion-Dollar Businesses
do: Publish or ship five imperfect pieces of the work you are avoiding today instead of polishing one.

said: What you accomplish is a direct output of the volume of activity that you do, multiplied by the leverage of the activity itself.
source_title: TBPN Live — Alex Hormozi's Playbook
do: Write one page naming today's highest-leverage task, then spend the next two uninterrupted hours only on that task.

said: You have to pick the right boat.
source_title: TBPN Live — Alex Hormozi's Playbook

source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022

said: He said you can have the relationship with a child that you want if you are willing to make the sacrifices that produce respect and reliability.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
takeaway: Give your kid your full attention
do: Spend one uninterrupted hour with your child, or a younger person in your care, doing what they asked for.

said: He said a vision of the relationship you want has to be concrete enough that you would recognize it if it showed up.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
takeaway: Say what you want in love
do: Write five lines about the relationship you want, each one a behavior, and do the first line today.

said: He described a badly damaged woman who asked to walk someone worse off than herself, and he took that as proof that service is still possible when you have almost nothing.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: Take one person who is worse off than you for a walk, a meal, or a finished errand today.

said: He said there is nothing better than putting out what you truly believe and learning that it helped someone else.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: Send one honest note to a person your work has touched, and say the true thing without polishing it for effect.

said: He asked whether time outside work would be used in a way that is productive, generous, and meaningful.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: Block one hour after work for a generous act you named in advance, and keep the block.

said: You have to be wise enough to govern your current behavior in light of the future, and that's really what it means to be an adult.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: Name one urge you would usually follow tonight and leave it undone because of the man you mean to be next year.

said: He told his daughter, while she was very ill, not to use the illness as an excuse to become bitter.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
takeaway: Don't use pain as an excuse
do: Name the hardship you have been using as today's excuse and complete one duty you would have skipped because of it.

said: He said you do not sacrifice a real pleasure unless you have something clearly better to put in its place, and that this is why a mere prohibition so often fails.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: Skip one drink or one scroll tonight and spend that same stretch on the better thing you wrote down this morning.

said: He said you treat other people as you would wish to be treated if you were treating yourself properly, which is not the same as granting every whim.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: Do one hard kindness for yourself that the man you will be next month would thank you for, then stop at that.

said: He said that at the crossroads the temptation is either to collapse into bitterness or to inflate yourself, and that neither one is the aim.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: At the next choice today, take the option that serves someone besides your image, and finish it before you sleep.

said: Try to create something elegant and concise.
source_title: Essays: Instructions and Topics
do: Write one page today and cut it until each sentence says only what it is supposed to say.

said: First, write a seven to ten sentence summary. Each sentence should carry enough conceptual weight to withstand elaboration into a paragraph.
source_title: Essays: Instructions and Topics
do: Outline one idea you care about in seven to ten sentences, each strong enough to become its own paragraph later.

said: Put the essay aside. After a delay (a day or more is optimal, as it is worthwhile to sleep at least once in the interim), write another outline, without referring to your first draft.
source_title: Essays: Instructions and Topics
do: If you drafted something yesterday, write a fresh outline from memory today and only then reopen the draft.

said: Do not be afraid to throw out ideas that now seem superfluous.
source_title: Essays: Instructions and Topics
do: Delete one passage, plan, or possession today that no longer serves the point.

said: Pick an idea that is clearly of interest to you. Analyze that idea.
source_title: Essays: Instructions and Topics
do: Spend one hour writing on one idea that is actually yours, not a summary of what you were handed.

said: Make your essays original. We are not merely looking for a summary or outline.
source_title: Essays: Instructions and Topics
do: Take one thing you have only summarized and add one original claim you are willing to defend in a page.

said: He told students that a piece of writing stands or fails at the sentence, the paragraph, and the whole, and that each word has to be chosen on purpose.
source_title: Essays: Instructions and Topics
do: Edit one paragraph in three passes today: the words, then the sentences, then whether the paragraph is a single idea.

said: He wrote that writing is a formalized kind of thinking that lets you draw a cause from an important event and then steer what you do now.
source_title: The Benefits of Writing
do: Write for fifteen minutes on one event that still snags you, and end with the cause you will act on before tonight.

said: He said that if an institution is broken, that is the work: go fix it, and the person who fixes one thing is then trusted with the next.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: Finish one small shared mess you can actually touch today, a hallway, a team document, or a neighbor's errand.

said: He asked graduates who they would be if they were a light to the people they work with, and said you can see when you deviate and correct it.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: Do one useful thing today for a colleague that is not your assignment, and do it without a speech.

said: He said each person has something to bring that no one else can bring, and that refusing that duty takes something out of the world.
source_title: At a Crossroads, Hillsdale College commencement, 2022
do: Do the one piece of your own work that only you can do today, and do not hand it off.

said: I don't have days like that. I pretty rarely have a day like that, but if I feel it happening and I catch myself within a few hours, then I do something radical with my body because the body will change the mind the fastest.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018
do: When the afternoon goes flat, do ten hard minutes of something physical before you try to think your way through the work.

said: I know that trying to think my way through it is not going to do squat.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018
do: Stop the mental loop for one bout of cold water, lifting, or a fast run, then come back and do the one task.

said: So I jump on that thing for 10, 12 minutes first thing in the morning and get my lymph moving.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018

do: Write one decision you have been blaming on circumstances, and put the first action on today's calendar.

source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018
do: Make three small decisions before noon that you have been postponing, and do the first step of each.

said: The most successful leaders are the ones that have to make decisions where they're likely maybe going to be wrong.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018

said: Beliefs create and beliefs destroy.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018

said: Knowledge has got to be converted to action or it's worthless.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018
do: Take one thing you already know you should do and finish the first physical step before tonight.

said: Life is always happening for us, not to us. It's our job to find out where the benefit is.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018
do: Write one sentence on what today's setback is forcing you to do that you have been avoiding.

said: So you and I have to figure out what it is that really lights us up, because success without fulfillment to me is the ultimate failure in life.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018

said: If your relationship is not growing, it is shrinking, it is dying.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018
do: Do one thing today that grows a relationship, a conversation or a real favor, and do not announce why.

said: Actually trade your expectations for appreciation and your whole life changes in a moment.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018

said: When we start to suffer we have a 90-second rule. Feel it for 90 seconds, figure it out, and let it go.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018

said: Kill the monster while it's a baby. Don't wait until it's Godzilla eating the city.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018
do: Handle the small irritation in the first hour instead of rehearsing it all afternoon.

said: You get in your head, you're dead.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018
do: Put both hands on your chest for two minutes, name three moments you are grateful for, and then write the next action.

said: You can't be grateful and angry simultaneously.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018

said: Maybe read, but I won't write or speak about something I'm not totally passionate about.
source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018

source_title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Tony Robbins on Achievement Versus Fulfillment (#178), 6 June 2018
takeaway: Feel the pain, skip the story

source_title: On Purpose with Jay Shetty: Tony Robbins on Three Steps to Lasting Change (transcript), 5 January 2026

source_title: On Purpose with Jay Shetty: Tony Robbins on Three Steps to Lasting Change (transcript), 5 January 2026

source_title: On Purpose with Jay Shetty: Tony Robbins on Three Steps to Lasting Change (transcript), 5 January 2026

source_title: On Purpose with Jay Shetty: Tony Robbins on Three Steps to Lasting Change (transcript), 5 January 2026

source_title: On Purpose with Jay Shetty: Tony Robbins on Three Steps to Lasting Change (transcript), 5 January 2026

source_title: On Purpose with Jay Shetty: Tony Robbins on Three Steps to Lasting Change (transcript), 5 January 2026

do: Stay where you are today and change one habit in place, instead of planning a trip to feel different.

source_title: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 40, translated by Richard Mott Gummere

do: Write one good memory of someone you have lost, and tell a living person one thing you loved about them.

source_title: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 75, translated by Richard Mott Gummere
do: Send one plain message today in the voice you would use on a walk, with nothing performed in it.

source_title: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 76, translated by Richard Mott Gummere

do: Do one favor today for someone who did not thank you last time.
